summary: The study describes the atomic layer deposition (ALD) of ultrathin copper metal films using a novel copper(I) amidinate precursor and molecular hydrogen as a reducing agent. The process enables the deposition of highly conductive, conformal copper films in high aspect ratio structures, with low impurity levels and good adhesion. The copper precursor is a liquid during vaporization due to its low melting point, ensuring reproducible vapor pressure and controllable transport. The ALD process is suitable for applications such as seed layers in microelectronics.
evidence: We report a method for producing thin, completely continuous and highly conductive copper films conformally inside very narrow holes with aspect ratios over 35:1 by atomic layer deposition. Pure copper thin films were grown from a novel copper amidinate precursor, copper N,N-di-sec-butylacetamidinate, and molecular hydrogen gas as the reducing agent. The copper precursor is a liquid during vaporization because its melting point is lower than its vaporization temperature. The growth per cycle varied from 1.5–2 Å/cycle on SiO2 or Si3N4 surfaces but was only 0.1–0.5 Å/cycle on metallic Ru, Cu, and Co surfaces. On oxide surfaces, copper atoms form isolated copper crystallites that merge into rough polycrystalline films after more deposition cycles. On Ru and Co metal surfaces ALD Cu nucleates densely, forming smooth and strongly adherent films that are continuous even for films as thin as 4 atomic layers. With 4 nm Cu deposited on 2 nm Ru substrates, the sheet resistance is below 50 Ω/□, which is low enough for making seed layers for electroplating Cu interconnect wires.
